title: Staged DNS TTL coordination lab notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working lab notebook for a controlled experiment to validate staged DNS TTL coordination during a region-level evacuation with warm-standby routing. The goal is to understand end-to-end convergence, client resolver behavior, and interaction with CDN edges and our own routing weights so we can produce a reliable operational playbook for gradual traffic migration and failback.

Scope and motivation:
- Trigger: simulated region capacity exhaustion (reserve region going into soft-evac mode).
- Target: ensure progressive traffic shift to warm-standby region(s) without causing request amplification, kv-cache cold starts, or client-side sticky routing blackholes.
- Focus on: DNS TTL settings across authoritative, CDN, and edge layers; authoritative TTL ramp-down strategy; TTL clamping by intermediaries; per-resolver retention; and metrics to observe safe migration.

Hypotheses:
1) Short authoritative TTLs alone (<= 30s) still result in multi-minute effective switchover due to ISP resolver caching and CDN clamp values (often 300s).
2) Staging TTL changes in 3 phases (announce intent, lower TTL, shift weights) reduces sudden backend load compared to single-step cutovers.
3) Pre-warming KV cache in target region using synthetic prefills reduces 95th/99th p99 tail latency during migration.

Experiment design (high level):
1) Baseline capture (30m): normal routing, TTLs, traffic distribution recorded.
2) Intent announcement (t+0): publish internal alert and set a 15-min hold window; no infra change. Observability wires: dashboards live.
3) Lower authoritative TTL (t+15m): change authoritative DNS from 5m to 30s for migrated host records, with documentation and versioned DNS change.
4) Wait (t+20m): allow for TTL propagation (best effort) and monitor resolver populations.
5) Warm cache prefill (t+25m): run controlled synthetic requests (low QPS) to populate KV/embedding caches in target region.
6) Weight shift in stages (t+30m onward): step routing weight increments 10% every 2 minutes, monitor errors/latency.
7) Observability window (t+0 to t+90m): high-frequency dashboards and runbook checklist.
8) Failback plan: if any abort criteria, revert weights and raise TTL back to baseline (5m) and trigger cache decay plan.

DNS & CDN details:
- Authoritative: Route53 hosted zone for redwood-inference.com; record set uses weighted routing by region set at 100/0 initially.
- Edge/CDN: Our CDN (third-party) has an enforced min-ttl of 300s for certain types; we have a support ticket to whitelist short TTLs for our anchor records (linked_artifacts above).
- Client side: Common resolvers observed: Google Public DNS, Cloudflare, ISP resolvers in NA/EMEA. Past telemetry shows Google respects short TTLs fairly quickly, some ISPs clamp to 5m-15m.
- A note on CNAME chains: anchor hostnames that include CNAME -> cdn.example.net sometimes cause TTLs to be taken from the final target. We need to be mindful which record to change.

Operator checklist (pre-execution):
- [ ] Confirm open support ticket with CDN to respect our sub-60s TTL for the experiment (ticket INF-2378).
- [ ] Coordinate with product feature team to avoid user-facing churn (announce maintenance window internally).
- [ ] Confirm synthetic prefill job parameters and keys (Ravi).
- [ ] Snapshot DNS zone and export change plan (Jonah).
- [ ] Open ephemeral monitoring channel in #sre-runs and alerting paging enabled with lower thresholds for 5xx and p95.

Metrics to watch (real-time):
- Region request qps per region (region-qps.{region}).
- 5xx rate by region and route (errors.per_route.5xx). Abort if 5xx rate > 1.5x baseline for > 2 minutes during a weight step.
- P95 and P99 latency for generate and chat endpoints (latency.generate.p95). Abort if p99 > baseline + 200ms for > 3 minutes.
- KV cache hit ratio in target region (kvcache.hit_ratio.target). If hit_ratio < 0.6 after prefill, pause and run additional prefill.
- Origin CPU/GPU saturation (node.cpu and gpu.util). Abort if any host > 80% sustained for > 60s.
- DNS resolver population heatmap: sample counts of resolvers still pointing to source region (resolver-cohort.count).
- Client-side retries and amplification (client.retries.per_min). Abort if retry storms observed causing >2x inbound QPS to origin.

Step-by-step runbook (detailed):
1) T+0: Baseline capture. Verify dashboards show green, note baselines explicitly in runbook channel with screenshots.
2) T+15m: Change authoritative TTL. Command: aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch file://ttl-lower.json. TTLs changed to 30s for A/CNAME records for api.redwood-inference.com targeted for migration.
3) T+20m: Query resolver population (script) to map which resolvers still resolve to old IPs. Command (example): ./scripts/dns-resolver-scan --domain api.redwood-inference.com --sample 1000. Output: CSV of resolver IP and returned IP. Expect >60% compliant before stepping weights.
4) T+25m: Run prefill job: kubectl run kv-prefill --image=redwood/kv-prefill:canary --args="--target-region=us-west-2 --keys-file=samples/critical_keys.txt --rate=50rps". Monitor kvcache.hit_ratio.target metric.
5) T+30m: Begin weight shift. Use orchestration console: routing-set api-route -> weight from us-east-1:100 -> us-west-2:0. Steps: set to 90/10 -> wait 2m -> 80/20 ... until 0/100. Use automation if available: platform routing CLI: rcli set-weight --route api-route --from us-east-1 --to us-west-2 --step 10 --interval 120s.
6) On each step: confirm error and latency thresholds; run quick end-to-end tests (login + generate). If thresholds exceeded, run abort.
7) After reach 100% target region: maintain high monitoring for 30m, then increase TTL back to 300s for stability unless otherwise decided.

Abort criteria and immediate actions:
- Abort if 5xx rate > 1.5x baseline over 2 minutes: rollback to previous weight and pause for diagnostics.
- Abort if p99 latency spike > baseline +200ms for 3 minutes: roll back and initiate cache analysis.
- Abort if KV cache hit_ratio < 0.6 after 10 minutes of prefill step: halt and run additional prefill.
- Abort if origin host GPU utilization > 80% for > 60s: pause to add capacity or scale.
- If abort: reverse weights to last known-safe state. Re-increase authoritative TTL back to 300s to allow resolvers to stabilize. Post-mortem to capture root cause.

Observed issues during lab (notes from run 2025-03-18):
- CDN min-ttl override: despite change to 30s, CDN returned cached responses with 300s TTL for ~14 minutes. This matched hypothesis #1; open ticket to CDN to fully honor our route-specific short TTLs.
- Resolver lag in a subset of APAC ISPs: some ISPs held old A records for 20+ minutes, leading to skewed traffic distribution and unexpected origin load.
- Prefill effectiveness: prefill raised kvcache hit_ratio to ~0.72 in 12 minutes at 50rps; however, some large keys still experienced cold loads due to eviction policies. Consider prioritizing top-500 keys by footprint.
- Client retry amplification: one client SDK performed aggressive retry without exponential backoff; during a weight step this generated spikes to origin causing transient CPU pressure. Action: reach out to partner to update SDK and add per-client rate limiting at edge.

Telemetry queries used (examples for quick-reuse):
- P95 latency: sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="generate",le="0.95"}[1m])) by (region)
- KV cache hit ratio: 100 * (sum(kvcache_hits{region="us-west-2"}) / sum(kvcache_requests{region="us-west-2"}))
- Resolver population: dns_resolver_sample_count{domain="api.redwood-inference.com"} by (resolver_cohort)

Conclusions & Recommendations:
- Do not rely on authoritative TTL alone. CDN and ISP clamp behavior make short TTLs less effective in the wild; staged approaches are needed.
- Prefill is effective but must target high-footprint keys; increase initial prefill rate and prioritize heavy keys.
- Add a short-lived, edge-level per-client rate limiter to protect origin during transitional steps to avoid amplification from misbehaving SDKs.
- Update runbook to include explicit CDN TTL validation step and require CDN whitelist prior to any production short-ttl change.
- Consider a hybrid approach: DNS weight changes + immediate routing-level weighted shifts (for clients behind compliant resolvers) together with a grace period where both regions serve overlapped traffic but with lower per-request concurrency to prevent origin saturation.

Open action items:
- INF-2378: CDN support for sub-60s TTL for api.redwood-inference.com (Ravi)
- Platform PR #982: add automated prefill job to routing shift automation (Jonah)
- Add runbook section for per-client rate limiting and SDK outreach (Elena)
- Schedule next full-scale rehearsal once CDN ticket confirmed and prefill automation merged.

Notes to self / unresolved questions:
- How do modern mobile carriers treat CNAME TTLs differently than A records? We should run a focused probe against mobile resolvers.
- Should we version edge config to allow rapid clamp override? Need WG with CDN provider.
- Investigate whether our global load balancer can perform weighted shifts at TCP level independent of DNS to speed safe migration.

Appendix: quick command snippets used during lab:
- Route53 TTL change: aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch '{"Changes":[{"Action":"UPSERT","ResourceRecordSet":{"Name":"api.redwood-inference.com","Type":"A","TTL":30,"ResourceRecords":[{"Value":"203.0.113.12"}]}}]}'
- Resolver scan: ./scripts/dns-resolver-scan --domain api.redwood-inference.com --sample 2000 --output resolver-scan-20250318.csv
- Start prefill: kubectl create job kv-prefill-20250318 --image=redwood/kv-prefill:canary -- sh -c 'python prefill.py --region us-west-2 --keys top500.txt --rate 100'

End of lab notes.

-- Marta (on-call SRE)
